name: Mulberry
lede: Mulberry is named for the fruit of the mulberry tree, and for centuries it meant a dark purplish red; on a screen today it is a brighter, pinker magenta.

sections.title: The swatch and the word
sections.body:
The swatch here is the modern screen mulberry, a strong magenta-leaning red-pink [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary lists the name, with a first record of 1776, and ISCC-NBS has a block for it [1]. The xkcd survey value for the same name is much darker, near #920A4E [1].

That darker reading is closer to the old word. Paterson defines mulberry simply as the color of the mulberry, also called mulberry red, and notes Dickens put Job Trotter in a "mulberry suit" in *The Pickwick Papers* [2]. His entry for murrey is the clue to how the dictionary sees it: a dark purplish red, a shortened form of mulberry [3].

sections.title: Murrey, morello and the Latin fruit
sections.body:
English kept two older words for the color. Murrey is mulberry cut short, and morello is a dark red that Paterson calls similar to murrey [3][4]. Some sources treat the two as the same color, others do not [3].

The Pigment Compendium traces morello to *morum*, the Latin word for mulberry, and groups it with *pabonazo* and *violetto* as Italian names for a purple [5]. It suggests the color may have been made from kermes or cochineal insects [5]. The fruit gave several languages the same dark, wine-like word for a color that sits between red and violet [3][5].

sections.title: A color painters could not agree on
sections.body:
In 1661 the heraldic writer C. F. Menestrier complained that painters did not know how to render the heraldic tincture called purple [6]. Some used a mauve and some a wine color. Others used the color of mulberries, which he described as a dark violet, and others the lighter color of the husk of mulberries [6].

The mulberry was therefore a reference color that even specialists used in two shades, one dark and one pale [6]. That is the same uncertainty a modern reader meets between a dark murrey and a bright screen swatch.

sections.title: In the dye trade
sections.body:
In the cloth trade the word named a dyed result. Greenfield notes that fine woolens called scarlet were sometimes dyed other colors, producing mulberrys, grays, blacks and even greens, and that in some places these were still sold as scarlets [7]. Color words in the cloth trade named a material and a quality as much as a hue [7].

Balfour-Paul counts mulberries among the medieval dyer's results when woad was paired with madder, kermes or even a lichen purple, alongside purples, pinks, violets and scarlets [8]. Woad is blue and madder and kermes are red, so these mixed dyes sit between red and violet, which fits a purplish red [8]. Compare [[madder]], the red half of that pair, and [[crimson]] and [[scarlet]], the other reds the trade named for their dyes [7][8].

sections.title: The tree and the silk
sections.body:
The color comes from the fruit, but the tree has its own history. Silkworms feed on the leaves of the white mulberry, *Morus alba*, and the leaves of that tree are about the only food they can eat without getting sick [9]. James VI and I wanted an English silk industry, and in 1607 owners of large estates were told to plant ten thousand mulberry trees each; a four-acre garden was planted where Buckingham Palace stands today, tended by the King's Mulberry Men [10]. Finlay reports that the king was wrongly advised, because most of the trees sent from France were black mulberries, and silkworms do not like their leaves [10].

Ancient story gives the fruit a color too. As Finlay retells Ovid, the lovers Pyramus and Thisbe die under a mulberry tree, and their blood turns its white fruit red [11]. It is a poet's tale, not botany. See the [[flower:mulberry|mulberry tree]] for the plant itself.

sections.title: Mulberry yellow
sections.body:
Not every old mulberry was red. The Pigment Compendium lists "mulberry" as a name for a yellow, and sends the reader to fustic [12]. The confusion is botanical: the tree that gives fustic, now called *Maclura tinctoria*, was once classed as *Morus tinctoria*, and the Boyle reference to a yellow dye from mulberry trees seems to come from that older name [12]. Young fustic is a different plant altogether, *Cotinus coggyria* [12].

So a recipe that mentions mulberry dye needs checking: it may mean a red-purple fruit color, or a yellow wood dye [12].

sections.title: A dark food
sections.body: In 1884 Huysmans opened *À rebours* with a funeral banquet at which every dish and drink was black, brown or purple [13]. Pastoureau quotes the menu, and mulberries are on it beside plum pudding and heart-cherries [13]. The fruit stands for a dark, nearly black purple, not for the bright pink of the swatch [13][12].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in just one painting, dated 1900, which makes the color rarer than 86 per cent of the named colors [14]. That is a screen-color measure of a bright magenta-red, which painters used sparingly; the darker murrey of the old word is not what this swatch tests [14][1].

In printed English, the adjective *mulberry* peaks in the 1830s, and by the 2010s its use is about a seventh of that peak [15]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings and a book-scan curve, so read them as hints, not as proof of a dye [14][15].

openers: Murrey, an old English color word, is just "mulberry" cut short: a dark purplish red.
"Mulberry yellow" was a real dye name, and it points to fustic, not to the fruit.
